nameStory: The Pickerelweed Shortface gets its name from its close relationship with pickerelweed plants, where it specializes in collecting pollen and nectar. The 'shortface' part refers to its distinctively short proboscis (tongue) compared to other bees, which is perfectly adapted for the shallow flowers of its favorite plant. This intimate plant-bee partnership has shaped both its common name and its entire lifestyle.
description: The Pickerelweed Shortface is a small, solitary native bee that specializes in visiting pickerelweed flowers along wetland edges. About the size of a honeybee worker but more slender, it has a dark metallic sheen with subtle bronze or greenish highlights that shimmer in sunlight. Unlike social bees that live in colonies, each female digs her own small nest burrow in sandy soil near water. These bees are part of the sweat bee family, though this species rarely shows interest in human perspiration.

idTips.label: Metallic sheen
idTips.description: Dark body with a subtle bronze-green metallic luster that catches light like a tiny jewel, especially noticeable when the bee moves between sun and shade

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Honeybee-sized but noticeably more slender and delicate-looking, with a streamlined appearance that seems built for quick, darting flights

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Fast, direct flight with quick hovering pauses at flowers, often making a soft buzzing sound higher in pitch than a bumblebee

idTips.label: Pollen-carrying behavior
idTips.description: Females carry dry pollen on specialized hairs under their abdomen rather than in leg baskets, creating a fuzzy yellow or purple patch on their belly

idTips.label: Antenna length
idTips.description: Relatively short antennae that don't extend much beyond the head when folded back, giving the face a compact appearance

habitat: Look for these bees around freshwater wetlands, pond edges, and slow-moving streams where pickerelweed grows in shallow water. They nest in sandy or loose soil within 100 yards of their host plants, often choosing gentle slopes with good drainage and morning sun exposure. You'll find them most commonly in areas where wetlands meet upland sandy soils.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not active yet. Look for small, pencil-diameter holes in sandy soil near water as signs of emerging nest sites from the previous year.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from mid-July through August when pickerelweed is blooming. Watch for fast-flying bees working the purple flower spikes, especially on warm, sunny mornings.
seasonality.fall: Activity winds down by early September as pickerelweed flowers fade. Late-season individuals may visit asters and other fall flowers near wetlands.
seasonality.winter: Overwintering as larvae in underground nest cells. No adult activity, but nest holes may still be visible in protected sandy areas.

funFact: This bee is so specialized that it times its entire life cycle to pickerelweed's bloom period - if the flowers are late due to weather, the bees will actually wait in their nest burrows rather than emerge early, sometimes delaying their appearance by weeks to match their favorite plant perfectly.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small dark sweat bees, but the Pickerelweed Shortface's consistent presence around wetlands and pickerelweed flowers is a dead giveaway. Memory trick: 'Pickerel in the pond, bee nearby' - if you see pickerelweed blooming, scan for the metallic glint of these specialized visitors.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'sweat bee,' this species shows little interest in human perspiration, unlike some of its relatives. The name comes from its family classification rather than its behavior. Many people don't realize that most of our native bees are solitary specialists like this one, not colony-living generalists.
compareHints: The closely related Beebalm Shortface is nearly identical in appearance but sticks to upland areas where wild bergamot and other mint-family plants grow, rarely venturing to wetlands. If you're near water and pickerelweed, you're almost certainly looking at the Pickerelweed Shortface. Both species have the same metallic sheen and size, but their habitat preferences make identification straightforward.
